reproduction_number_range.source: Mills et al. 2004 (PMC7095078): 1918 median 2, interquartile 1.7 to 2.3, 2.7 over fastest growth; Biggerstaff et al. 2014: 1918 median 1.80, interquartile 1.47 to 2.27. The two studies differ by a few tenths; the file's 1.5 to 2.7 spans both.

transmissibility_per_day.source: Reproduction number 2.0 divided by the infectious days; not itself observed

case_fatality.source: Wikipedia, Spanish flu (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_flu, opened, table of major influenza pandemics): case fatality rate '2-3%' for 1918, other estimates about 4% or 10%; 0.02 is the low end of that table. Copenhagen's combined mortality was 0.29% of the population, on about a third infected.

immunity.source: Wikipedia, Spanish flu (opened): older adults 'may have had partial protection caused by exposure to the 1889-1890 flu pandemic', 28 years before 1918, and survivors of the first wave 'had become immune' to the second within months. Protection therefore lasts from years to decades but is partial and strain-specific; the 10-year waning here is a ballpark inside that, not a measured duration.

stage.latent.source: Mills et al. 2004 (PMC7095078): assumed mean latent period 1.9 days; shape 2 is a derived choice

stage.infectious.source: Mills et al. 2004 (PMC7095078): assumed mean infectious period 4.1 days; shape 2 is a derived choice

density_exponent.source: Heuristic inside the range Rader et al. 2020 (Nature Medicine, abstract read: crowded cities see longer epidemics with larger attack rates; scaling weaker than linear) supports; the report gives no exponent per route. Respiratory person-to-person contact sits mid-range; vary across the ensemble
